final.rationale: I used a 12-predictor logistic regression on all 1,700 patients, with median imputation for missing values. Every predictor is known at admission. It has 26.3 events per model column, which is enough for logistic regression. Five-fold cross-validation gave AUC 0.732 ± 0.029, PR-AUC 0.531 ± 0.036 (a model with no skill scores 0.232) and Brier 0.146. That is modest discrimination: useful for ranking risk, but not accurate enough to decide care for one patient alone. I compared it with three other models. A 21-predictor logistic model scored AUC 0.724 and PR-AUC 0.527. Gradient boosting on the same 21 predictors scored AUC 0.711 and PR-AUC 0.510. An L1-penalized logistic model with 34 candidate predictors scored AUC 0.732 and PR-AUC 0.539, with Brier 0.145. The penalized model has the same AUC and a slightly higher PR-AUC, but the differences are within the fold-to-fold noise. I chose the simpler logistic model because it is easier to interpret. The nonlinear boosting model did no better, which suggests the signal is mostly additive. The main risk factors are a history of chronic heart failure (stage I in particular), older age, diabetes, lateral MI extent, and atrial fibrillation at admission. The prior-heart-failure odds ratio is very large because that category is small, so treat its size cautiously. The protective odds ratio for cardiogenic shock at admission is based on few patients and is unlikely to be causal. It may reflect early death before heart failure could develop, or the way the outcome was recorded. Pulmonary edema, hypertension stage, sex and prior MI count were not significant after adjustment. Odds ratios are associations, not causal effects. The data come from a single hospital in 1992-1995, and the model has not been validated externally.

Every predictor is known at admission. It has 26.3 events per model column, which is enough for logistic regression. Five-fold cross-validation gave AUC 0.732 ± 0.029, PR-AUC 0.531 ± 0.036 (a model with no skill scores 0.232) and Brier 0.146. That is modest discrimination: useful for ranking risk, but not accurate enough to decide care for one patient alone. I compared it with three other models. A 21-predictor logistic model scored AUC 0.724 and PR-AUC 0.527. Gradient boosting on the same 21 predictors scored AUC 0.711 and PR-AUC 0.510. An L1-penalized logistic model with 34 candidate predictors scored AUC 0.732 and PR-AUC 0.539, with Brier 0.145. The penalized model has the same AUC and a slightly higher PR-AUC, but the differences are within the fold-to-fold noise. I chose the simpler logistic model because it is easier to interpret. The nonlinear boosting model did no better, which suggests the signal is mostly additive. The main risk factors are a history of chronic heart failure (stage I in particular), older age, diabetes, lateral MI extent, and atrial fibrillation at admission. The prior-heart-failure odds ratio is very large because that category is small, so treat its size cautiously. The protective odds ratio for cardiogenic shock at admission is based on few patients and is unlikely to be causal. It may reflect early death before heart failure could develop, or the way the outcome was recorded. Pulmonary edema, hypertension stage, sex and prior MI count were not significant after adjustment. Odds ratios are associations, not causal effects. The data come from a single hospital in 1992-1995, and the model has not been validated externally."}
